Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Understand key technical aspects of reverse shoulder arthroplasty for the management of
rotator cuff arthropathy.
Review preoperative considerations for reverse shoulder arthroplasty.
Discuss critical surgical steps and intraoperative considerations for successful reverse
shoulder arthroplasty.
Gain an appreciation of the long-term outcomes and potential complications of reverse
shoulder arthroplasty for the management of rotator cuff arthropathy.
Rotator Cuff Arthropathy
Background

Neer first described the clinical and pathologic findings of rotator cuff tear arthropathy in
1983.1

Rotator Cuff Arthropathy
Neer described the importance of the rotator cuff in preventing superior migration of
the humeral head. In describing the pathology associated with rotator cuff arthropathy,
Neer noted proximal migration of the humeral head, rounding of the greater tuberosity,
rupture of the long head of the biceps, thinning of the humeral head cartilage, and
erosion of the undersurface of the acromion.1 These are the characteristic pathologic
findings of advanced rotator cuff arthropathy that continue to be observed in many
patients with rotator cuff tear arthropathy.
In 1985, Grammont introduced the reverse shoulder prosthesis indicated for patients
with rotator cuff arthropathy as described by Neer. This innovative design moved the
center of rotation of the shoulder to a more inferior and medial position in relation to
the native glenohumeral joint center of rotation.2 As a result, the deltoid lever arm is
lengthened, and the deltoid can function to achieve forward elevation of the shoulder
without a well-functioning rotator cuff (Resource 1).
Preoperative Evaluation and Patient Selection
Patient History
Most patients with symptomatic rotator cuff tear arthropathy will present with a combination
of shoulder pain, weakness, and decreased range of motion.

Patient History
Patients with rotator cuff arthropathy have symptoms of lateral-sided shoulder pain that
often are present at night and increased with overhead activities. Many patients will

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001063
2/27

report pain with reaching out to the side and difficulty with overhead use of the
shoulder.
Physical Examination
Physical examination findings consistent with rotator cuff pathology include decreased range
of motion and decreased strength at the involved shoulder.

Physical Examination
During physical examination, inspection of the skin about the shoulder for surgical
incisions from previous procedures, such as arthroscopic or open rotator cuff repair, is
important. Patients with rotator cuff arthropathy often present with lack of full forward
elevation and, in some instances, pseudoparalysis of the shoulder. Pseudoparalysis is
broadly defined as active forward flexion of the shoulder of less than 90° with preserved
passive forward elevation.3 Weakness with abduction and external rotation is common.
Surgeons must assess for an external rotation lag sign and/or a positive hornblower
sign. A considerable external rotation lag sign and/or a positive hornblower sign may
indicate the need for reverse shoulder arthroplasty (RSA) in combination with latissimus
dorsi tendon transfer.4 Assessment for intact deltoid and axillary nerve function is
important because deltoid insufficiency is an absolute contraindication to RSA.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs are necessary to evaluate patients with shoulder pain and rotator cuff
arthropathy.
A classification system commonly used to characterize the progression of rotator cuff tear
arthropathy is the Favard classification (Figure 1).


Imaging Studies
Radiographs should include AP, true AP, and axillary views. Although not always critical,
a scapular Y view can be obtained to assess posterior subluxation that may not be fully
apparent on an axillary view.
A representative true AP radiograph indicative of advanced rotator cuff arthropathy is
shown in Figure 2. Note the proximal migration of the humeral head with loss of
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001063

glenohumeral joint space.
The Favard classification system defines the progressive erosive glenoid changes that
occur in patients with rotator cuff arthropathy. This classification describes four types of
glenoid wear patterns in rotator cuff arthropathy: E0 to E3. E0 is defined by proximal
migration of the humeral head without erosion of the glenoid, E1 is defined by
concentric wear of the glenoid, E2 is defined by wear of the superior aspect of the
glenoid, and E3 is defined by a wear pattern that has progressed to involve the superior
and inferior aspects of the glenoid.

Advanced Imaging Studies
Advanced imaging studies, such as a CT scan, are helpful for preoperative planning.

Advanced Imaging Studies
CT scans can be obtained to better assess glenoid bone loss and for preoperative
planning, which can be performed via various preoperative planning software programs.
MRI typically is not required for patients with advanced rotator cuff arthropathy because
the diagnosis of rotator cuff deficiency in patients with cuff tear arthropathy often can be
made via a clinical examination and plain radiographs alone.
Surgical Technique
Patient Positioning
Patients are carefully placed in the beach-chair position.

Patient Positioning
The patient is placed in the modified beach-chair position or the beach-chair position
with cervical spine alignment maintained in a neutral position5 (Figure 3). Surgical
extremity must be positioned such that the medial border of the scapula is free from the
edge of the surgical table because this will allow for full extension of the humerus and
will aid in humeral exposure intraoperatively.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:04 PM

modified beach-chair position with cervical spine alignment held in neutral. (Reproduced
from Chalmers PN, Van Thiel GS, Trenhaile SW: Surgical exposures of the shoulder. J Am
Acad Orthop Surg 2016;24[4]:250-258.)
Surgical Exposure
The two most commonly used approaches for RSA are the superolateral approach and the
anterior deltopectoral approach.5 The preferred approach of the author of this lesson is the
deltopectoral approach (Figure 4; Video 1).

TB, eds: Surgical Techniques in Orthopaedics: Controversies in Proximal Humeral Fractures [DVD].
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2014.
The coracoid process is palpated and marked as a landmark for the deltopectoral interval. The
interval between the deltoid and pectoralis can be easily palpated in most patients. For the
deltopectoral approach, an 8- to 10-cm skin incision is made along the deltopectoral interval,
starting at the coracoid process and directed toward the deltoid insertion.
The initial surgical dissection passes through three distinct layers to reach the glenohumeral
joint. Layer one is the deltopectoral interval, layer two is composed of the clavipectoral fascia,
and layer three includes the subscapularis and the anterior capsular structures of the
glenohumeral joint.

Surgical Exposure
Full-thickness skin flaps are raised medially and laterally to allow for adequate
visualization of the fat stripe that identifies the interval between the deltoid and
pectoralis. The cephalic vein is identified just deep to the fat stripe, and blunt dissection
can be performed to reflect the cephalic vein laterally with the deltoid. In patients with
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:04 PM
AAOS | Rotator Cuff Arthropathy: Reverse Shoulder Technique and Outcome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001063
9/27

rotator cuff arthropathy, adhesions in the subacromial and subdeltoid plane must be
carefully released. The upper 1 cm of the pectoralis major insertion also may be released
to facilitate exposure.
A blunt self-retaining retractor is placed to reflect the pectoralis and deltoid to expose
the clavipectoral facia. The clavipectoral fascia is incised lateral to the conjoined tendon.
The axillary nerve can then be palpated deep to the conjoined tendon. Identification of
the axillary nerve in this manner helps to protect it throughout the procedure. The
anterior humeral circumflex vessels are ligated and cauterized. A blunt self-retaining
retractor can then be placed deep to the conjoined tendon to expose the subscapularis.
Management of the subscapularis depends on the condition of the subscapularis and
surgeon preference. Subscapularis peel, tenotomy, or lesser tuberosity osteotomy may
be performed to address the subscapularis during RSA. Along with the subscapularis, the
capsule and humeral attachments of the glenohumeral ligaments are released along the
anterior and inferior aspect of the anatomic neck of the humerus. The humeral head is
exposed and can then be dislocated via a combination of external rotation, extension,
and adduction of the humeral shaft.
Humeral Head Osteotomy
Before dislocation of the humeral head, the self-retaining retractor that was previously placed
under the conjoined tendon must be removed to avoid injury to the brachial plexus.
After the humeral head is exposed and the shoulder is dislocated, the humeral head
osteotomy is performed.

Humeral Head Osteotomy
A humeral head osteotomy is performed with the use of an intramedullary guide or via a
freehand technique, matching the angle of inclination of the implant system being used.
Retroversion of the humeral head osteotomy is set between 0° and 40° of retroversion.

Figure 5 shows a retroverted humeral head cut. The forearm and the posterior rotator
cuff attachments are referenced in determining appropriate retroversion.
Postoperative external and internal rotation may be influenced by variations in
retroversion of the humeral component. After the humeral head osteotomy has been
performed, the glenoid can be exposed.

Glenoid Exposure
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:04 PM
AAOS | Rotator Cuff Arthropathy: Reverse Shoulder Technique and Outcome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001063
11/27

Adequate exposure of the glenoid is critical to well-performed RSA because the surgeon
requires unobstructed access to the glenoid for optimal glenoid instrumentation and implant
placement.

Glenoid Exposure
A wet Ray-Tec sponge is placed to protect the deltoid muscle and cephalic view. The
subdeltoid space must be mobilized and released to open the scapulohumeral interface.
Posterior glenoid rectors are placed. Commonly used retractors include small Bankart
retractors, a Darrach retractor, or a Fukuda retractor. Retractors are placed at the
posterior rim of the glenoid, and the humeral head is gently retracted posteriorly and
inferiorly to expose the glenoid. In patients with advanced rotator cuff arthropathy, the
subscapularis may not be adequate for repair. If the subscapularis is of good quality and
is amenable to repair, complete subscapularis releases are performed. The superior
glenohumeral, middle glenohumeral, and inferior glenohumeral ligaments are released
to allow for full excursion of the subscapularis and to facilitate optimal glenoid exposure.
After mobilization of the subscapularis, a Bankart retractor is placed along the anterior
rim of the glenoid. Complete labral excision is performed to allow for visualization of the
entire glenoid. Excision of the inferior labrum and release of the inferior capsule from
the inferior aspect of the glenoid are critical because this will allow for visualization of
the inferior glenoid rim. Care must be taken to protect the axillary nerve during inferior
capsular releases. A Cobb elevator may be used to remove any residual cartilage from
the face of the glenoid.
Glenoid Instrumentation
Glenoid instrumentation depends on the system being used; however, fundamental principles
should be followed to achieve optimal baseplate support and fixation, including achieving
maximal baseplate support on native glenoid bone while preserving subchondral bone and
obtaining maximal screw fixation.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001063
12/27


Glenoid Instrumentation
With the glenoid fully exposed, attention is focused on positioning and instrumentation
of the baseplate. The inferior aspect of the glenoid is referenced to avoid placing the
baseplate too high on the glenoid. Inferior positioning of the baseplate is preferred to
avoid adduction and external rotation impingement, which may lead to scapular
notching and/or instability.6 Care is taken to avoid superior tilt of the baseplate because
this may lead to instability and shear forces across the baseplate that may compromise
fixation.
The guide pin is placed through the guide and then advanced through the far cortex of
the glenoid vault Figure 6.
Instrumentation then proceeds based on the system being used. If reaming, the reamer
should be started off the bone to prevent glenoid fracture. Regardless of the system
being used, the goal of baseplate fixation is to achieve maximum baseplate support and
maximum screw fixation while minimizing overreaming, which may lead to substantial
violation of the subchondral bone. After reaming is completed, the baseplate is then
inserted and the central post or central screw is engaged. Compression of the baseplate
on the native glenoid face must be achieved. After adequate compression is achieved,
locking screws are inserted in the peripheral holes. The inferior screw should be directed
along the scapular neck, and the superior screw should be directed toward the base of
the coracoid to avoid a trajectory that may result in injury to the suprascapular nerve.
The desired glenosphere is then impacted to the baseplate to engage the taper fixation.
Regardless of the system used, confirmation of full seating of the glenosphere on the
baseplate is critical.

Humeral Preparation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:04 PM
AAOS | Rotator Cuff Arthropathy: Reverse Shoulder Technique and Outcome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001063
14/27

Humeral preparation is completed in a stepwise manner after placement of the glenoid
components. Care must be taken to avoid overreaming the humeral canal.
Humeral fixation often is achieved via press-fit fixation; however, cementation occasionally is
necessary.

Humeral Preparation
After insertion of the glenoid components, the proximal humerus is delivered from the
wound and the humerus is exposed by placing the arm in external rotation and
extension. This provides exposure to the cut surface of the proximal humerus. An entry
reamer is used to gain access to the humeral canal. The humeral head center lies
posterior and medial to the humeral shaft center and the entry point to the humeral
canal.7
Sequential reaming is performed. Reaming is stopped at the first sign of endosteal
contact. Overreaming should be avoided because this may lead to periprosthetic
fracture. Line-to-line reaming is recommended, and care should be taken to avoid
overreaming because this may decrease the time-zero fixation of the humeral
component.8 The trial broach is placed, with version set between 0° and 40° of
retroversion. The author of this lesson prefers 20° of retroversion; however, 0° to 40° of
retroversion is acceptable. Increased retroversion will lead to increased postoperative
external rotation, whereas retroversion closer to 0° will lead to increased postoperative
internal rotation. With the trial stem in place, the thinnest polyethylene liner is selected,
and the shoulder is reduced. Appropriate length-tension relationships are confirmed,
and the shoulder is taken through range of motion. Confirmation of no adduction or
external rotation impingement that may lead to subsequent instability or scapular
notching is important.
After provisional reduction is confirmed, the shoulder is dislocated again, and the trial
humeral components are removed. At this time, nonabsorbable sutures may be passed
through bone tunnels in the proximal humerus for later subscapularis repair. The final
stem is impacted to the humerus. Press-fit fixation often is achieved; however, if poor

bone quality is present or if adequate press-fit fixation cannot be achieved, the author of
this lesson recommends cement fixation of the humeral stem.
Polyethylene Liner Selection
Trialing and selection of the polyethene component should occur after the final humeral stem
has been placed. Selection of the appropriate polyethylene liner depends on soft-tissue length-
tension relationships and intraoperative stability.

Polyethylene Liner Selection
With the final stem in place, multiple polyethylene liners are trialed to select the optimal
liner based on intraoperative stability, range of motion, and soft-tissue length-tension
relationships. Soft-tissue tension is first evaluated by ensuring that no undue tension is
present on the axillary nerve or the conjoined tendon. With gentle axial traction on the
arm, the amount of translation, or shuck, between the glenosphere and the polyethylene
liner can be determined. Although achievement of stability is critical, overlengthening
should be avoided because it may lead to nerve injury, persistent postoperative pain,
and acromial stress fracture.9,10 Range of motion also should be evaluated because
intraoperative range of motion is predictive of postoperative range of motion.11
Surgeons should confirm once more that no adduction or external rotation impingement
is present because this may lead to post-impingement instability and/or scapular
notching.12 After the appropriate polyethylene liner is selected, it can be impacted to the
stem. The shoulder is then reduced, and the subscapularis can then be repaired. A
layered closure is then performed. The author of this lesson obtains postoperative
radiographs to ensure no immediate postoperative complication, such as fracture or
dislocation, is present (Figure 7).

Postoperative Management
Postoperative management includes a period of immobilization followed by progressive range
of motion activities.

Postoperative Management
Immediately postoperatively, the patient’s arm is placed in a sling with an abduction
pillow. The sling is maintained for 3 to 6 weeks postoperatively; however, elbow, wrist,
and hand range of motion is permitted. The patient should remain non–weight bearing
and is instructed to avoid lifting more than 5 lbs for the first 4 weeks. After the first
month, the sling may be discontinued, and the patient begins home pulley exercises
focused on gradually increasing shoulder range of motion. In the experience of the
author of this lesson, formal physical therapy often is not required to regain optimal
shoulder range of motion in patients with rotator cuff arthropathy who undergo RSA.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:04 PM

Patients continue with home pulley exercises until 3 months postoperatively, at which
time they may return to many of their normal activities. The author of this lesson
recommends avoiding higher level activities, such as golf, tennis, and other recreational
sports, until 4 months postoperatively.
Outcomes of RSA
Early research on long-term outcomes of patients with rotator cuff arthropathy who
underwent RSA showed 95% implant survival at a follow-up of 9 yearsin.13 However, Guery et
al13 demonstrated lower implant survivorship for patients who underwent RSA for other
etiologies, such as trauma. In addition, the authors raised concerns about performing RSA in
younger, more active patients given the observed decreased functional outcome scores in
their cohort with longer term follow-up.
RSA in younger, more active patients is controversial given more recent literature on the
subject.
Recent long-term follow-up studies on RSA for the management of rotator cuff arthropathy
have shown improvements in functional outcomes and low revision surgery rates 10 years
postoperatively.

Outcomes of RSA
Ernstbrunner et al14 evaluated the long-term results of RSA in patients younger than 60
years who had a massive, irreparable rotator cuff tear. The authors reported substantial
improvements in pain, range of motion, and overall functional outcomes after 10-year
follow-up. They found these results to be durable without deterioration of functional
outcome beyond 10-year follow-up.14 Despite these promising results, the authors
reported a complication rate of 39%, noting that patients with complications had inferior
subjective and objective postoperative outcomes.
Cuff et al15 reported on a cohort of 94 patients who underwent RSA, with midterm (5-
year) and long-term (10-year) follow-up. The authors found that patients had substantial
improvements in functional outcome scores, improved range of motion, and a low

revision rate.15,16 At 5-year follow-up, the mean forward flexion improved from 64°
preoperatively to 144° postoperatively, with an overall implant survival rate of 94%.16 At
10-year follow-up, improvements in functional outcome measures were maintained, and
range of motion improvements were similar to those reported at 5-year follow-up. The
implant survival rate remained promising at 90% at 10-year follow-up.15
Kennon et al17 reported on the long-term outcomes of 100 patients who underwent RSA.
The authors found the 10-year cumulative incidence of revision surgery to be
approximately 6%. In addition to a low revision rate, the authors also reported
substantial improvements in forward elevation across the cohort at long-term follow-up.
Complications
Although more recent literature has demonstrated excellent results after RSA, with a low
overall revision rate, complications may occur after RSA (Resource 2).
The most common complications after RSA include scapular notching, dislocation, acromial
fracture, nerve injury, glenoid loosening, and infection.18
Scapular Notching
Although the clinical importance of scapular notching is controversial, it is reported in many
studies as the most common complication after RSA.18,19

Scapular Notching
Scapular notching refers to the resorption of the inferior aspect of the lateral pillar of the
scapula medial and superior to the inferior rim of the glenoid baseplate. The etiology of
scapular notching is multifactorial and is influenced by patient anatomy, glenoid wear
pattern, implant design, and intraoperative component positioning. Scapular notching
has been shown to be more common in patients with rotator cuff arthropathy compared
with patients with arthritis and rotator cuff deficiency.20 Lévigne et al20 found that
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:04 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001063
19/27

superior glenoid erosion, such as that in patients with an E2 glenoid, increased the risk
for scapular notching. Intraoperative factors that contribute to scapular notching include
superior position of the baseplate and glenosphere and a more valgus neck-shaft angle
of the humeral component.6,21
The clinical importance of scapular notching is unclear based on the current literature.
Sirveaux et al22 found that the rate of scapular notching was 64% in 80 patients after
RSA. In this study, patients with advanced scapular notching had decreased clinical
outcomes compared with those with less severe scapular notching. This is in contrast to
other studies, which have not shown a correlation between functional outcome and
scapular notching after RSA.23,24
Dislocation
Instability is one of the more common complications after RSA. A systematic review of
complications after RSA reported a cumulative incidence of dislocation of 4.7%.19

Dislocation
A more recent study reported a dislocation rate of 9.2% after primary RSA.25 Cheung et
al25 found that dislocations occurred a mean of 8 weeks postoperatively. The authors
also reported risk factors for instability, including male sex, previous open shoulder
surgery, preoperative diagnosis of fracture sequalae, and lack of subscapularis repair.
Kohan et al26 reviewed a cohort of 19 patients with instability after RSA and described
two distinct etiologies for instability. The authors concluded that instability after RSA was
likely caused by inadequate soft-tissue tensioning or instability from impingement or
liner failure.26 Treatment options for dislocation after RSA include closed versus open
reduction and revision RSA. Chalmers et al27 reported on a series of patients with
instability within 3 months of index RSA. In this cohort of patients with early dislocation,
the authors found that closed reduction alone was successful in 44% of patients,
whereas 45% required polyethylene liner exchange.

Acromial Fracture
Acromial spine fractures can occur after RSA and are associated with an overall incidence of
approximately 4% after RSA.28,29 The etiology of acromial stress fractures is multifactorial and
has been attributed to osteoporosis, increased glenoid offset, smaller humeral lateral offset,
increased arm lengthening, and a thinner acromion.10

Acromial Fracture
Zmistowski et al28 reported on 958 patients who underwent RSA with a minimum follow-
up of 3 months to determine the incidence and predictors of acromial spine fractures
after RSA. The authors reported the incidence of acromial stress fracture to be 4.2%,
with an additional 6.4% of patients having an acromial stress reaction. Time to symptom
onset was a mean of 8.8 months after RSA. The authors found that female sex,
decreased change in deltoid length, and increased preoperative glenohumeral center of
rotation medialization were independent predictors of acromial stress pathology.
Acromial stress fractures remain a challenging complication to manage after RSA.
Reported treatment options include nonsurgical and surgical management, including
open reduction and internal fixation.30 Regardless of management, functional outcomes
are decreased in patients with acromial stress fractures who had a previously well-
functioning RSA implant.29
Nerve Injury
The incidence of nerve injury after RSA has been reported to be between 1% and 2%.19,31 The
etiology of nerve injury after shoulder arthroplasty is multifactorial and may be caused by
nerve injury during surgical dissection, traction injury during exposure and arm positioning,
hematoma formation, cement extrusion, and nerve blocks.32

Nerve Injury

Laadermann et al9 investigated the incidence of neurologic injury after reverse and
anatomic shoulder arthroplasty. In their cohort, RSA was associated with a higher rate of
nerve injury compared with anatomic shoulder arthroplasty. The authors suggested that
the relative arm lengthening after RSA that is required to allow for appropriate soft-
tissue tensioning may lead to increased nerve injuries after RSA.9 A retrospective review
of 211 patients undergoing shoulder replacement identified additional risk factors for
nerve injury after shoulder arthroplasty. RSA was associated with the highest risk of
nerve injury, and female patients and patients who underwent previous surgery of the
affected shoulder had a higher risk of nerve injury. Most nerve injuries that occur after
RSA are transient in nature.9,32
Glenoid Loosening
Glenoid component loosening is a rare complication after RSA and can be minimized via
adequate baseplate support and fixation. As further advances in RSA implants are made, the
rate of glenoid loosening is likely to continue to decrease.

Glenoid Loosening
Frankle et al33 reported on the short-term follow-up of 60 patients who underwent RSA.
The authors found the rate of glenoid loosening to be 11.7%; however, modification of
the baseplate design to include peripheral locking screw fixation has substantially
decreased the rate of glenoid loosening at long-term follow-up.16 With the use of most
contemporary implants, the rate of glenoid loosening is reported to be less than
5%.13,15,16,22
Infection
Infection remains a concerning complication after RSA and is estimated to occur with an
incidence of approximately 3.8%.19 Similar to other shoulder surgical procedures, the most
common infecting organism is Cutibacterium acnes.23,31

Infection
Management of deep infection subsequent to RSA involves surgical management via
irrigation and débridement during one- or two-stage revision.34,35 The decision to
proceed with one- versus two-stage revision is based on the virulence of the causative
organism, patient factors, and the acuity of the infection. Regardless of surgical
management, combined treatment via systemic antibiotic agents also is recommended.
In some patients, an antibiotic spacer may be placed and left indefinitely and is
considered a definitive antibiotic spacer.36
